name: Erythrokeratoderma Variabilis Progressiva

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Histopathological Diagnostic Criteria for EKVP

criteria.description: Presence of transient erythematous patches with fixed hyperkeratotic plaques
Skin biopsy showing hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and papillomatosis without significant inflammation
Identification of pathogenic variants in GJB3 or GJB4 genes
Positive family history consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of characteristic clinical presentation and histopathological findings; genetic testing supportive but not mandatory
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical supported by histopathology; genetic confirmation aids but absence does not exclude diagnosis

pathognomonic.notes: Erythematous patches change location over hours to days
Typically symmetrical distribution on extremities and trunk
searchTerms: thickened scaly plaques with clear edges

pathognomonic.notes: Thickening of skin on palms and soles

common.symptomName: Scaling and fissuring of hyperkeratotic areas
common.notes: May lead to discomfort and secondary infection risk
searchTerms: scaly and cracked thick skin areas

common.notes: Lesions commonly affect both sides of the body
searchTerms: lesions appearing evenly on both sides
skin spots on both sides of body

common.symptomName: Onset in infancy or early childhood
common.notes: Typically presents within first year of life
searchTerms: signs appearing in babies or young kids

occasional.symptomName: Erythematous patches exacerbated by heat or stress
occasional.notes: Environmental factors may trigger lesion changes
searchTerms: red skin patches worsened by heat

occasional.notes: Due to fissuring and skin barrier disruption
Thickened or brittle nails occasionally observed

rare.symptomName: Mild palmoplantar pain due to fissures
rare.notes: Pain related to fissuring in thickened skin
searchTerms: mild pain in palms and soles
pain from cracks in skin on hands and feet

rare.notes: Rarely, vesicles or blisters may form

laboratory: Skin biopsy showing hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, papillomatosis without significant inflammation
genetic: Pathogenic variants in GJB3 (connexin 31) or GJB4 (connexin 30.3) genes
other: Family history consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance

distinguishingFeatures: Predominantly fixed plaques with fewer migratory erythematous patches
Symmetric hyperkeratotic plaques without migratory erythema
Later onset in childhood or adolescence

redFlags: Rapid progression of skin lesions with ulceration
Signs of secondary bacterial infection (e.g., fever, purulence)
Severe palmoplantar fissuring causing functional impairment
references: Boyden LM, et al. Mutations in GJB3 and GJB4 cause erythrokeratodermia variabilis. Nat Genet. 2002.
Hennies HC, et al. Genetic heterogeneity of erythrokeratodermias. J Invest Dermatol. 2004.
